pattern.summary: 9 questions, attempt any 5, each carries 20 marks. No compulsory question. Roughly half the paper is theory and half is numerical problems.

choosing: Q9 (computerised accounting / Tally) is theory and often lets you pick two of three notes — a reliable choice.
numerical: Draw proper T-accounts or formats with Dr/Cr and dates. Show the balancing figure clearly.
Write working notes for every calculation (interest, loading, closing stock) — they earn marks on their own.

topics.name: Computerised Accounting & Tally
topics.summary: Usually the last question (Q9), always theory, often 'write notes on any two'. The most predictable 20 marks in the paper.
points: Computerised accounting: recording transactions with software. Merits: speed, accuracy, automatic ledger posting and reports, easy storage. Demerits: cost, need for training, data security and virus risk, power/system failure.
Manual vs computerised: recording (hand vs software), speed, accuracy, reports (prepared vs generated instantly), storage (books vs files), cost.
Choosing accounting software: cost, ease of use, flexibility and scalability, data security, vendor support and training, compatibility with existing systems, statutory compliance (GST).
Tally company creation: Gateway of Tally → Create Company → name, address, financial year, books beginning date.
Ledger vs group: a ledger is an individual account (e.g. Ram, Rent); a group is a collection of similar ledgers (e.g. Sundry Debtors). Tally has 28 predefined groups (15 primary, 13 sub-groups).

Vouchers: Contra (F4), Payment (F5), Receipt (F6), Journal (F7), Sales (F8), Purchase (F9), Credit Note, Debit Note. Post-dated vouchers are recorded now but affect books only on their date (e.g. post-dated cheques).
Stock item = a single product; stock group = items of similar nature (e.g. Mobiles); stock category = a parallel classification across groups (e.g. by price range or use).
Reports: Balance Sheet, Profit & Loss, Trial Balance, Day Book, Cash/Bank Book, Stock Summary, Ratio Analysis — available from Gateway of Tally → Display.
topics.frame: Definition (2–3 lines) → 5–6 headed points with one line each → a small comparison table where relevant → one-line conclusion.
mistakes: Writing only definitions — each 10-mark note needs 5–6 distinct points.
Mixing up stock group and stock category.

topics.name: Branch Accounts
topics.summary: Either a numerical (Branch Account / Stock & Debtors system) or theory on systems of dependent branches.
points: Objectives: find profit/loss of each branch, control stock and cash, assess branch performance, help decide expansion or closure.
Types: dependent branches (HO keeps the accounts), independent branches (keep their own books), foreign branches.

Dependent branch systems: (1) Debtors system — a Branch Account works like a Nominal account; (2) Stock and Debtors system — Branch Stock, Branch Debtors, Branch Expenses, Branch Adjustment and Branch P&L accounts; (3) Final Accounts system — a trading and P&L account per branch.
Goods at invoice (selling) price: the loading (profit element) is removed through Branch Adjustment Account so only real profit is recognised.
Branch Stock Account at invoice price acts as a memorandum control: the balancing figure shows shortage or surplus of stock.
Branch fixed assets kept at HO: HO records purchase and charges depreciation to the branch.
Reasons HO account and branch account differ: goods or cash in transit, expenses charged by HO not yet recorded by branch, errors.
method: Debtors system: open Branch A/c. Debit: opening stock, opening debtors, petty cash, prepaid expenses, goods sent, cash sent for expenses. Credit: cash remitted by branch (cash sales + collections), goods returned to HO, closing stock, closing debtors, closing petty cash.
Liabilities work the other way: opening outstanding expenses on the credit side, closing outstanding expenses on the debit side.
Credit sales, discounts, bad debts and returns by customers do NOT enter the Branch Account (they are inside the debtors figure).
If goods are sent at invoice price: bring stock and goods sent at invoice price, then remove loading with contra entries (Stock Reserve / Goods sent to Branch).
Balancing figure of Branch A/c = profit (credit shortfall) or loss.
formula: e.g. cost + 25% → loading = 25/125 = 1/5 of invoice price
mistakes: Putting credit sales in the Branch Account under the debtors system.
Forgetting to remove loading on opening and closing stock.

topics.name: Joint Venture
topics.summary: Recently as a full numerical (Memorandum JV + JV with co-venturer's account) and as theory on methods.
points: Joint venture: a temporary partnership of two or more persons for a specific venture, ending when the venture is complete. No firm name, co-venturers share profit in agreed ratio.
JV vs Partnership: temporary vs continuing; specific venture vs ongoing business; no firm name; Partnership Act applies to partnership.
JV vs Consignment: co-venturers are co-owners vs principal–agent relationship; profit shared vs commission; account sales not needed in JV.
Methods WITHOUT separate books: (1) each co-venturer records all transactions; (2) each records only his own transactions + a Memorandum Joint Venture Account.
Method WITH separate books: Joint Venture Account, Joint Bank Account and Co-venturers' Personal Accounts.
method: Memorandum JV Account (= a P&L of the venture): Debit all expenses and goods bought by all venturers; credit sales and stock/assets taken over. Balance = profit, shared in ratio.
'Joint Venture with X Account' in A's books: Debit A's own purchases/expenses and A's share of profit; credit A's own sales and goods A takes over. Balance = amount due to/from X, settled by cash.
Separate books: Joint Bank A/c (contributions in, payments out), JV A/c (all expenses, sales, profit), Co-venturers' A/cs (contribution + profit share − withdrawals).
formula: Profit share = JV profit × agreed ratio
mistakes: Recording the other venturer's transactions in 'JV with X' account under the Memorandum method.
Forgetting stock or plant taken over by a venturer on the credit side.

topics.name: Hire Purchase & Instalment
topics.summary: Theory on features and hirer's accounting, numericals with default and repossession.
points: Hire purchase: goods are delivered at once, ownership passes only after the last instalment. Hirer can return the goods; vendor can repossess on default.
Instalment purchase: ownership passes at once; buyer cannot return; vendor can only sue for dues.
Rights of hirer: use the goods, terminate by returning goods, buy by paying all dues early, get notice before repossession.
Hirer's books: record asset at full cash price; interest is revenue expense; depreciation on full cash price.
Goods of small value: Hire Purchase Trading Account method or Stock and Debtors system.
method: Find interest per instalment: interest = rate × outstanding cash price (work backwards when cash price is not given).
Asset A/c Dr (full cash price) To Vendor A/c.
Each instalment: Interest A/c Dr To Vendor A/c; then Vendor A/c Dr To Bank A/c.
Depreciation on full cash price each year; interest and depreciation to P&L.
Default and repossession (hirer): Vendor A/c Dr To Asset A/c (with the amount still due); the rest of the returned goods' book value is a loss on repossession, transferred to P&L.
formula: Interest = Opening balance of cash price × Rate
Total interest = Hire purchase price − Cash price
mistakes: Charging depreciation on the instalments paid instead of full cash price.
Deducting interest from the down payment.

topics.name: Consignment
topics.summary: Numericals on Consignment Account and valuation of unsold stock, theory on invoice price, loading and losses.
points: Consignment: goods sent by the consignor (owner) to a consignee (agent) who sells them on commission. Ownership stays with the consignor.
Proforma invoice: a statement sent with goods showing quantity and price — not a sale.
Account sales: statement sent by the consignee showing sales, expenses, commission and the balance due.
Del credere commission: extra commission paid to the consignee who takes the risk of bad debts.
Invoice price: goods sent above cost to hide profit from the consignee; loading removed by adjustment entries (goods sent, returns, opening and closing stock).
Normal loss is absorbed in cost of good units; abnormal loss is valued at cost and credited to Consignment A/c, debited to Abnormal Loss A/c (insurance claim to be deducted).
method: Consignment A/c (Dr): goods sent, consignor's expenses, consignee's expenses, commission. (Cr): sales, abnormal loss, closing stock. Balance = profit/loss.
Unsold stock value = (Cost of goods + consignor's expenses + consignee's non-recurring expenses) × unsold units ÷ units received.
Consignee's selling expenses (godown rent, selling) are NOT added to stock value.
Commission: ordinary on total sales; over-riding on surplus above invoice; del credere on total credit sales.
formula: Closing stock = (Total cost incl. direct expenses) ÷ Units received × Units unsold
Normal loss: units received = sent − normal loss
mistakes: Adding selling expenses to closing stock.
Treating normal loss as abnormal loss.

topics.name: Trial Balance, Errors & Rectification
topics.summary: Usually a 20-mark rectification with Suspense Account.
points: Trial balance: a list of ledger balances to check arithmetical accuracy. Objectives: check accuracy, summary for final accounts, locate errors.
Limitations: errors of omission, commission, principle and compensating errors do not affect agreement.
Types of errors: omission, commission, principle, compensating. Errors affecting trial balance go through Suspense Account.
method: For each error, write what was done, what should have been done, then the correcting entry.
If the error affects only one account (e.g. wrong posting, casting error), use Suspense A/c for the other side.
If both sides are wrong (e.g. entered in wrong book), no suspense — correct both accounts.
Post all suspense entries to Suspense A/c; it must close to zero.
formula: Undercasting of Sales Book → Suspense A/c Dr To Sales A/c
Overcasting of Purchase Book → Suspense A/c Dr To Purchases A/c
mistakes: Using suspense for errors that don't affect the trial balance.
Reversing the sign of casting errors.

topics.name: Depreciation
topics.summary: Mostly a 20-mark theory question on meaning and methods; sometimes a Machinery Account numerical.
points: Depreciation: permanent, gradual and continuous fall in the value of fixed assets due to use, time or obsolescence.
Factors: cost of asset, estimated useful life, scrap value.
Need: correct profit, true value of assets in balance sheet, funds for replacement, legal requirement.
Depletion (wasting assets like mines), amortisation (intangible assets), obsolescence (becoming outdated).
Methods: Straight Line / Fixed Instalment, Written Down Value / Diminishing Balance, Annuity, Sinking Fund, Insurance Policy, Machine Hour, Depletion.
SLM: simple, same charge each year; ignores falling repairs. WDV: higher charge early, balances with repairs, accepted by income tax, never reaches zero.
method: Machinery A/c: purchase cost + installation; depreciation each year (pro rata for part years).
On sale: find book value on date of sale; profit/loss = sale price − book value; transfer to P&L.
mistakes: Not charging depreciation for the part year before sale.
Leaving out installation charges from cost.

topics.name: Accounting Concepts, Conventions & Income
points: Concepts: business entity, money measurement, going concern, accounting period, cost, dual aspect, realisation, accrual, matching.
Conventions: consistency, full disclosure, conservatism (prudence), materiality.
Matching: expenses of a period are matched with the revenue of the same period to find true profit.
Income measurement principles: accounting period, realisation (revenue recognition), matching, accrual.
topics.frame: One-line meaning of each concept + one example each. For 20 marks, cover 8–10 concepts with examples.
mistakes: Listing names without examples.

topics.name: Accounting Process & Double Entry
topics.summary: Mostly 10-mark theory: double entry, rules of debit and credit, process, bases of accounting.
points: Double entry: every transaction affects two accounts with equal debit and credit.
Advantages: complete record, arithmetical check, profit and financial position known, fraud detection.
Golden rules: Personal — debit the receiver, credit the giver; Real — debit what comes in, credit what goes out; Nominal — debit expenses and losses, credit incomes and gains.
Accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Capital.
Accounting process: identify → record (journal) → classify (ledger) → summarise (trial balance, final accounts) → analyse and interpret → communicate.
Cash vs accrual basis: cash records only when paid/received; accrual records when earned/incurred.
topics.frame: Definition → features/advantages as headed points → a small example entry or table.

topics.name: Nature, Scope & Users of Accounting
points: Accounting: identifying, measuring, recording, classifying, summarising and communicating financial information.
Objectives: systematic records, find profit or loss, show financial position, provide information to users.
Users: owners, managers, investors, creditors, lenders, employees and trade unions, government, customers, public.
Qualitative characteristics: understandability, relevance, reliability, comparability (plus timeliness, verifiability).
Accounting information system: collects, processes and reports financial data for decisions.
topics.frame: Definition → objectives or users as headed points (one line each, what each user wants) → conclusion.

topics.name: Accounting Standards (AS, Ind AS, IFRS)
topics.summary: Mostly 10-mark theory: objectives, procedure in India, Ind AS vs IFRS.
points: Accounting standards: written policy documents on recognition, measurement and disclosure of transactions.
Objectives: uniformity, comparability, reliability, reduce alternatives, credibility.

Procedure in India (ASB of ICAI): identify area → study group prepares draft → exposure draft circulated for comments → revised draft → approved by ICAI Council → notified by Central Government (with NFRA/NACAS recommendation).
IFRS: issued by IASB, global standards. Ind AS are IFRS-converged standards notified for Indian companies (with some carve-outs).
topics.frame: Definition → objectives → steps as a numbered list → comparison table where asked.

topics.name: Final Accounts
topics.summary: Trading & P&L / Balance Sheet numericals and format questions.
points: Trading A/c: opening stock, purchases − returns, direct expenses vs sales − returns, closing stock → gross profit.
P&L A/c: indirect expenses and losses vs gross profit and other incomes → net profit.
Balance Sheet: assets and liabilities in order of liquidity or permanence; vertical format for companies (Schedule III).
Manufacturing A/c: raw materials consumed + direct wages + factory overheads ± WIP → cost of production.
Asset types: fixed, current/floating, liquid, fictitious (e.g. preliminary expenses), wasting (e.g. mines).
method: Classify each item: direct (Trading) vs indirect (P&L) vs balance sheet.
Carriage inwards/wages → Trading; carriage on sales, salaries, rent → P&L.
Apply adjustments before totalling.
formula: COGS = Opening stock + Purchases − Purchase returns + Direct expenses − Closing stock
mistakes: Putting carriage on sales in Trading A/c.
Forgetting closing stock on both P&L side (Trading credit) and Balance Sheet.

topics.name: Adjustments in Final Accounts
topics.summary: 20-mark theory question on the adjustments and their two-fold effect.
points: Closing stock: credit Trading A/c, asset in Balance Sheet.
Outstanding expenses: add to expense in P&L, liability in Balance Sheet.
Prepaid expenses: deduct from expense, asset in Balance Sheet.
Accrued income: add to income, asset. Income received in advance: deduct from income, liability.
Depreciation: debit P&L, deduct from asset.
Bad debts and provision for doubtful debts: debit P&L, deduct from debtors.
Interest on capital (expense) and interest on drawings (income).
topics.frame: Meaning of adjustment → each adjustment with its two effects (P&L side and Balance Sheet) — a table works well.
mistakes: Showing only one effect of an adjustment (every adjustment has two).

topics.name: Subsidiary Books (Cash Book, Purchase Book)
topics.summary: Cash book / purchases book numericals and 'why is the journal sub-divided'.
points: Journal is sub-divided to save time, allow division of work, reduce errors and give quick information.
Special books: Cash Book, Purchases Book, Sales Book, Purchases Returns, Sales Returns, Bills Receivable/Payable Books, Journal Proper.
Only credit purchases of goods go in the Purchases Book; trade discount is deducted in the book itself.
Petty cash book: small expenses under the imprest system.
method: Single column cash book: Dr receipts, Cr payments; balance c/d.
Cash discount appears in the discount column (two-column cash book); trade discount is never recorded.
Purchases Book: date, supplier, invoice no., details (qty × rate − trade discount + taxes/charges), amount.
mistakes: Recording cash purchases or asset purchases in the Purchases Book.
Recording trade discount in the accounts.

topics.name: Journal & Ledger
topics.summary: Rare as a full question, but journal entries are needed for every numerical topic.
points: Journal: book of original entry — transactions recorded date-wise with narration.
Ledger: accounts classified from the journal; balanced periodically.
Opening entry: Assets A/cs Dr To Liabilities and Capital A/c.
method: Identify accounts → classify (personal/real/nominal) → apply golden rules → write entry with narration.
mistakes: Missing narrations.
Recording trade discount.
